lawyer:
Syed Ishtiaque Ahmed, Additional Attorney-General K. Z. Alam, Deputy Attorney-General, M. Islam, Asstt. Attorney-General,  M. M. Haque, Asstt. Attorney-General ----- For petitioner. 
Syed Manzurul Ahsan with Mohammad Ainuddin, Advocates -----For Respondent No. 2.
Mozammel Huq, Advocate, Amicus Curaie.
parties:
General Manager, Hotel Intercontinental, Dacca ----- Petitioner.
Vs.
The Chairman, Second Labour Court, Dacca and another ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
(1) A dismissed worker is not a worker within t he meaning of this term as defined in Clause (xxviii) of section 2 of the Ordinance because a dispute between a single Worker and his employer regarding his dismissal is not an industrial dispute even though I may involve the question of employment or unemployment. I will become an industrial dispute when such dispute IS taken UP by the trade union of workers or by a number of workers. In support, reliance was placed by him upon a number of decisions. These are reported in AIR 1957 SC 104 and 532, AIR 1960 SC 777, AIR 1966 SC 182, (1962) 14 DLR 654, PLD 1962 Lah. 269 (1975) 27 DLR 70, 98 While interpreting the expressions industrial dispute" the courts of this sub-continent are thus seen to have introduced certain limitations. 

 (2) No dispute is an "industrial 'dispute" unless it is raised by toe collective bargaining agent, as provided by sections 26, 27(a) and 28 of the Ordinance. 

 (3) The remedy against dismissal, when such dismissal is not espoused and sponsored by the collective bargaining agent, has been provided by section 25 of the Act of.' 1965. The dismissed worker has, there fore no remedy under section 34 of the Ordinance, Section 34, which requires our consideration provides as follows:- 

 "Worker and "workman" mean any person not falling within the definition of employer who is employed (including employment as an apprentice) in an establishment or industry for hire or reward either directly or through a contractor whether the terms of employment be expressed or implied and for the purpose of any proceedings under this Ordinance in relation to an industrial dispute includes a person who has been dismissed discharged, retrenched, laid off or otherwise removed from employment in connection with or as a consequence of that dispute or whose dismissal discharge, retrenchment lay off, or removal has led to that dispute. 

 12. The definition of "workman" which has been held to be exhaustive [vide (1961) 13 D LR SC 280 at page 296] consists of two parts. The first part which concerns itself with the etymological sense of the term does not include a dismissed workman as he has ceased to be and is no. longer in employment. According to this definition, a workman whose services have been terminated can net also be included in it [vide (1974) 26 DLR 33]. The second part of the clause gives an extended meaning to the term "workman" and includes two. categories of dismissed workmen for a limited purpose, A "workman" whose dismissal was caused by an industrial dispute which already existed or whose dismissal had led to an "industrial dispute" is included within the second part of the definition. For the purposes of this Ordinance he can only figure in a proceeding which raises en industrial dispute, the existence of an industrial dispute, whether raised before or after his dismissal, is a condition precedent before a dismissed "workman" will fall within the definition. As in the present case, there was no industrial dispute in existence, either before or after his dismissal, the respondent No. 2 is net a "workman" within the meaning of this term as defined in the aforesaid clause. He is, therefore, net competent to file an application under section 34 of the Ordinance. 

 13. The learned Additional Attorney-General next proceeded to show that having regard to the scheme of the Ordinance and the language used in section 34, it was inconceivable that an industrial dispute can be raised under section 34. Section 34 itself does not contain the expressions "industrial dispute". He referred to the several provisions of the Ordinance regarding the raising of an industrial dispute which must be distinguished front an individual dispute raised by workmen. Section 26 of the Ordinance provides how an industrial dispute can be raised by initiating negotiations. Sections 27(a) to 30 provide the procedure of conciliation If both negotiations and conciliation fail and the parties do net agree to arbitration under section 31, the collective bargaining agent may resort to strike and the employer may resort to lockout as mentioned In section 32(2); the Government may prohibit the strike or lock-out if the strike or lock-out continue for more than 30 days. If the Government is satisfied that the strike or lock-out is causing serious hardship to the community or prejudicing national interest, then the Government may do so even before the expiry of 30 days, In case of public utility services the Government may before the expiry of 30 days prohibit the strike or lock-out. Section 32(3) provides that if the Government prohibits the strike or lock-out the Government is to refer the dispute forthwith to the Labour Court for adjudication. Section 32(4) provides that the Labour Court is to give its decision within the period of 60 days from the date when the reference was made. Under section 32(1-A) the parties to the dispute, whether before or the commencement of strike or lock-out, may jointly apply to the Labour Court for adjudication. The provision for such joint application has been made by an amendment. Excepting In the manner laid down as above for raising an Industrial dispute, no industrial dispute can be raised under any other section of the Ordinance. 

 14. The learned Additional Attorney-General therefore submitted that an industrial dispute can never be raised by a dismissed workman by merely filing an application under section 34 challenging his own dismissal. Since no industrial dispute was in existence prior to the filling of the application under section 34, such application by the respondent No. 2 is not maintainable. 

 15. Next, while expressing the view that the jurisdiction to decide an industrial dispute Which is conferred by the provisions of section 35(5) (a) is different from the jurisdiction to decide matters under section 34 which cannot be viewed as an industrial dispute, the learned Additional Attorney-General submitted that the words 'refer to' used in the former section relate to sections 32(2), 32(3) and the words 'brought before' relate to section 32(1)(A). The provisions of section 35(5)(a) are concerned with the adjudication of industrial dispute and those of section 35(5)(d) conferred jurisdiction with respect to matters under section 34. He further submitted that even when the unamended section 34 contained the words party to an industrial dispute, the provisions of section 35(5)(e) conferred jurisdiction to adjudicate upon matters included within section 34. In this connection he also stressed the difference which exists between adjudication of an industrial dispute and adjudication of a matter In relation to an industrial dispute. Section 34 deals with the latter kind of adjudication. By way of example he referred to the provisions of section 47 of the Ordinance which prohibits dismissal of a "workman" on grounds connected with an existing industrial dispute. If, however, a workman is dismissed during the continuance of an industrial dispute on any such ground the dismissed workman comes within the definition of workmen as given in Clause (xxviii) of section 2 and he can, therefore, file an application under section 34 for the enforcement of his right as provided by the aforesaid section. This kind of dispute will not be an industrial dispute but can be treated as an individual dispute in relation to an industrial dispute. Another instance may be when the collective bargaining agent takes up the case of a dismissed "workman" and starts negotiations and conciliation, the dismissed worker being a workman within the definition of Clause(xxviii) of section 2 can then claim reinstatement by filing an application under section 34, though the dispute raised by the collective bargaining agent will be an industrial dispute. The dispute which is raised under section 34 by the dismissed workman will thus be an industrial dispute in relation to an industrial dispute. The learned Additional Attorney-General conceded by saying that the provisions of section 41 cannot nullify the provisions of section 43 of the Ordinance which are mandatory. 

 16. He further submitted that prior to the enactment of the Ordinance in 1969, there was no means of enforcing the terms of an award or settlement except by raising a fresh industrial dispute. If a breach of such an award or settlement occurred when only payment of money was ordered under an award or settlement, such money would be realised as land revenue. Now under the Ordinance an award or settlement can be enforced by filing an application under section 34 without raising any fresh industrial dispute. 

 17. Finally, a comparison was made by the learned Additional Attorney-General between the provisions of section 25 of the Act of 1965 and those of section 34 of the Ordinance. These are, in his opinion, mutually exclusive. He submitted that when in violation of section 47 of the Ordinance a workman is dismissed he may ask for reinstatement by filing an application under section 34, the reason being that any violation of section 47 is not a matter covered by the aforesaid Act. He can, how ever move the Labour Court under section 34. Similarly, if an industrial dispute has been raised by the collective bargaining agent .over the dismissal of a workman the latter may file an application under section 34 of the Ordinance, for section 25(l)(b) of the Act of 1965 expressly provides that the Labour Court has no jurisdiction to adjudicate the matter under section 25 in respect of an industrial dispute which has been raised by a collective bargaining agent. In such cases the dismissed workman can file an application under section 34. He concluded by saying that a workman whose dismissal has not arisen out of or led to an industrial dispute cannot file an application under section 34 but can move an application under section 25 of the Act of 1965, for this Act is the only law which protects the worker against dismissal. 

 18. Mr. Syed Manzurul Ahsan, the learned Advocate who appeared on behalf of the respondent No.2, raised the following contentions in support of the view that an industrial dispute exists even when a dispute is raised or brought before the Labour Court by a single worker:- as dismissed worker being a worker within the definition of "workmen" provided in the Ordinance can bring a dispute relating to his non-employment before the Labour Court and such dispute will, therefore, be an industrial dispute. (2)A dismissed "worker" as defined in the Ordinance can maintain an application under section 34 read with sections 35 (5)(a) and 41(3)(a) of the Ordinance, since such a dismissed worker has no remedy under section 25 of the Act of 1965. Since he is not a workman within the definition of workmen provided in that Act, the only remedy appears to have been provided under section 34. 

 18A. as the contentions of the learned Advocate were similar to those raised by Mr. Mozammel Huq, the learned Advocate whom I called to assist the Court, and since Mr. Huq made elaborate. Submissions in support of such contentions we shall refer to them together, not separately. Before doing so it may, however, be mentioned that Mr. A.Y. Salehuzzaman, the learned Advocate for the petitioner in petition No. 798 of 1974 which was heard analogously with the present petition, made submissions in favour of the argument that a dismissed worker having fallen within the definition of workman or worker as provided in the Ordinance can maintain an application under section 34 even when there exists no industrial dispute has been raised by the collective bargaining agent. Need-less to say, his efforts to prove that a dispute raised by a single workman under section 34 of the Ordinance is an industrial dispute brought in for our consideration the same arguments so ably placed before us by the learned Amicus Curiae. 

 19. Mr. Mozammel Huq, who is one of the senior Advocates of this Court and whom I called to assist the Court in deciding the question whether a dispute between a single 'Work-man' and his employer relating to his dismissal is an industrial dispute or not, submitted as follows :— 

 I. Section 43 of the Ordinance controls the raising of a dispute by a collective bargaining agent in the manner as laid down in sections 26 to 28 and such raising of a dispute is the condition precedent to the reference of the dispute to Labour Court Section 43 does not control the bringing of a dispute under section 34 either by an individual worker or an individual employer or even by collective bargaining agent. 

 II. The dispute brought before a Labour Court by an individual worker, whether it relates to his dismissal or any other conditions of service is an 'Industrial Dispute' and as such decision under section 34 is an award, 

 III. Section 35(5)(a) is the only provision which creates jurisdiction for the Labour Court to adjudicate determine Industrial Dispute, both collective and individual, whether referred to or brought before it, either by a body of workers through collective bargaining agent or by an individual worker. A Labour Court will have no jurisdiction to decide any dispute under section 34 of the Ordinance unless it is an 'Industrial Dispute'. 

 20. In elaborating his submissions, he first referred to the definition of industrial dispute in clause (xiii) of section 2 of the Ordinance. In applying the principle of literal construction to this definition, it may be concluded that the words "workmen" and "employers" which are in the plural also include a single workman and a single employer for, according to section 13 of the General Clauses Act "unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context", words in the singular include the plural and vice-versa. But, in spite of the provisions in the General Clauses Act as above mentioned great controversy exists as to whether a dispute between an individual workman with his 'employer' is an industrial dispute or not. Referring to the decision in A. Roberio Vs. Member, Labour Appellate Tribunal, Dacca and another reported in (1975) 27 DLR 98 that since section 13 of the General Clause Act begins with the words unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context, the statute as a whole is to be read to ascertain the scheme and object of the statute before applying this section. Accordingly, it was submitted by him that wherever the context shows that it has been used with reference to a large number of workmen an individual worker is not meant, but where the context showed a singular number in respect of a dispute, such dispute is an industrial dispute within the definition provided in Clause XIII of section 2 of the Ordinance as section 34 of the Ordinance has used the word workman in singular, there is no reason why a dispute brought by a single workman will not be an industrial dispute. 

 "A Labour Court shall adjudicate and determine as Industrial Dispute which has been referred to or brought before it under this Ordinance. 

 This section, according to him, is the only provision in the Ordinance which has created the jurisdiction to adjudicate and determine an industrial dispute either referred to it or brought before it. Section 34 did not create any jurisdiction but only creates a forum for three categories of persons for ventilation of their grievances. In the unamended sec. 35(5)(a) the dispute brought before the Labour Court by an application under sec. 34 was expressly called an industrial dispute and the phrase "any party to an industrial dispute" which was used therein made any matter to be adjudicated under that section 'an industrial dispute'. After the amendment of this section this phrase has been replaced .by the words "any collective bargaining agent or any employer or workman" and this, according to the learned Advocate, has removed the difficulty. Created by section 43 He then submitted that the labour policy of the Government as reflected in the Ordinance divided industrial disputes into two classes namely; (i) matters of interests and matters of rights. For matters of interests procedure has been laid down for raising a dispute, for negotiation, for conciliation, for arbitration, for strike notice or lock-out and finally for reference to the Labour Court and the whole procedure is controlled by section 43 of the Ordinance. But for matters of rights no procedure has been laid down. The law simply says that it can be brought before a Labour Court for enforcement by a simple application and section 43 has no manner of application to a matter of right to be brought under section 34. Unfortunately this distinction is often lost sight of on account of the identity of definition and he submitted that this has also happened in the decision reported in (1975) 27 DLR 98. He further submitted that since 1969 the scope and scheme of the Ordinance became completely different from those of similar legislations in India. Indian decisions relied upon in (1975) 27 DLR 98 have no application to the law in Bangladesh. The Ordinance of 1969 has introduced some new concepts namely matters of interests and matters of rights, the concept of collective bargaining agent, the concept of bringing a dispute to a Labour Court by an individual worker instead of the same being referred to the Labour Court by the Government. Besides, provisions like sections 32(I)(A), 34, 35(5)(a), 49(I), 41(3) are completely absent in the Indian Legislation. 

 22. The learned Advocate referred to some Indian decisions reported in AIR 1949 Born. 141, AIR 1949 (F.C.). 111 and AIR 1954 All 516 which interpreted the definition of industrial dispute (which is the same as in the Ordinance) as including an individual dispute between a single worker and his employer. Reference was also made to an English case reported in (1951) 2 All England Report 828.in which, while interpreting the definition of (trade union) in Article 7 of the Conditions of Employment and National Arbitration Order, 1940, Lord Chief Justice Goddard held that the dispute between individual worker and his employer is a trade dispute. Trade dispute as defined in the said Article is as follows:— 

 "Any dispute or difference between the employers and workmen and work-men 	connected with employment or non-employment or the terms of employment or with 	condition of labour of any person. 

 "This definition was almost identical with the definition of 'Industrial Dispute' as provided in our  law. Mr. Huq submitted with great respect that in 27 DLR 98, the first part of the decision in (1951) 2 All England Report 828, was lost sight of. In the latter case there, in fact 2 decisions, one under the Conditions of Employment and National Arbitration Order, 1940 and another under Ankle 12 of the Industrial Dispute Order, 1951, which expressly said dispute does not include a dispute as to employment or non-employment of any person 9, As a result of the amendment in 1951 their Lordships said that an individual worker's dispute with his employer is not a trade dispute. This portion of the judgment has no application to our case inasmuch as no such change has been made in our law. It was, therefore, submitted with great respect that the actual-decision in (1951) 2 All England Report 828, has not been correctly reproduced in (1975) 27 DLR 98. Besides, the Indian decisions relied upon by the Division Bench in 27 DLR 98 have no application to our law since 1969 on account of the apparent differences between the scheme of our law and that of the Indian law. The scheme of the Indian law was such that the machinery of adjudication could not be set in motion by any individual worker where as our law expressly made provisions enabling an individual worker to set in motion the adjudication machinery. This is entirely consistent with the literal construction put on the definition of Industrial Dispute. 

 23. So far as section 25 of the Act of 1965 is concerned the learned Advocate submitted that it was intended to be an alternative remedy. In the opinion of the learned Advocate, since the definition of a worker in the Act of 1965 is very limited, a large number of persons who can claim to be a worker under the Ordinance will not be entitled to maintain an application under section 25 of the Act of 1965. He mentioned that for this reason it was rightly held in the decision reported in (1975) 27 DLR 98 that a dismissed workman, in view of the amendment of section 34 of the Ordinance, may file an application under this section. He also submitted that same views were expressed 10 an unreported decision of this Court in Omar Sons Ltd. V s, The Chairman, 1st Labour Court, Writ Petition No. 132 of 1971. In conclusion, section 25 of the Act of 1965 did not provide the only remedy for a dismissed worker. 

 24. Having referred to the various view-points expressed by the learned Advocate which I have incorporated quite extensively it is necessary to examine them and arrive at the conclusion whether the respondent No. 2 who is a dismissed worker was entitled to maintain an application under section 34 of the Ordinance. Views on this preliminary issue, as expressed by the learned Additional Attorney-General, are diametrically opposed to the views expressed by the learned Advocates including the amicus curiae. According to the former, any individual dispute as to "rights" can be raised by a worker under section 34 but since a dismissed worker is not a worker so far as an individual dispute is concerned, he is not entitled to make an application under the aforesaid section but is entitled to do so if the dispute is an industrial dispute which has been taken up by the collective bargaining agent as an industrial dispute. According to the latter,a dispute brought before a Labour Court under section 34 by a single worker is also an industrial dispute within the meaning of Clause (XIII) of section 2 of the Ordinance and, therefore, a worker who has been dismissed by his employer can maintain an application under the" aforesaid section challenging his dismissal. So far as the provisions of the unamended section 34 of the Ordinance are concerned, any party to an industrial dispute relating to a matter arising out of any right, guaranteed or secured to an employer or workmen by or under any law for the time being in force or an award or settlement may apply to the Labour Court for adjudication of the dispute. Leaving aside the consideration of the subject-matter for which an application could lie under the unamended provisions of section 34, it appears that whenever an industrial dispute arose "any party to such dispute", could file an application there under. 

 25. In deciding who is a party to an industrial dispute it would be first necessary to construe the words "industrial dispute", Whether an individual dispute which is not an industrial dispute would enable a worker to file an application under the unamended section was, therefore, to be determined with reference to the meaning of the words "industrial dispute." 

 26. As after the amendment of section 34 the words "industrial dispute" do no longer occur in this section, the question arises whether such dispute can be raised by filing an application thereunder. In place of "any party to an industrial dispute" as used in the unamended section 34, the expressions "any collective bargaining agent or any employer or workman" have been used. There is no reference to an industrial dispute or the adjudication of such dispute in the amended section 34. So far as a collective bargaining agent or an employer is concerned, it may maintain an application under this section whenever the necessity arises for the enforcement of any right guaranteed or secured to it by or under any law or any award of settlement for there is no dispute or controversy regarding the definition of a collective bargaining agent or an employer. Difficulty is however, experienced when a work-man applied under this section to enforce such a right. Such difficulty would riot perhaps have arisen had the definition of "worker" or "workman" as provided in clauses (xxviii) of section 2 of the Ordinance been a little simpler, clearer and more unambiguous. What appears to be the meaning of a "worker" or "workman" by taking a first glance at the definition is not seen to last long, particularly when the definition is subjected to minute scrutiny. The definition of "workers" or "workman" as given in Clause (xxviii) of section 2 of the Ordinance has classified them into two distinct categories. The two categories fall in two parts of the clause and are construction ally joined together by the use of the conjunction "and" which is preceded and followed by a comma. A "worker" or "workman" who falls in the first category means any person who is net an employer as defined in the ordinance but is employed for hire or reward under any express or implied term of employment, an apprentice would also fall in this category. In the second category falls a "worker" or "workman" who has been dismissed, discharged, retrenched, laid off or otherwise removed from employment, but, besides such dismissal, retrenchment or removal two other factors must exist so as to bring him under this category. One is the existence of any proceedings under the Ordinance in relation to an industrial dispute and the other is the existence of some connection between his dismissal, discharge, retrenchment, lay-off or removal and the industrial dispute. To be more explicit, his dismissal must have arisen out of an industrial dispute or must have led to such dispute. If the distinction between these two categories of workers or workmen has been intended by the legislature different consequences must necessarily follow from it If such distinction has been intended to exist between two categories of "workers" or "workmen" then a "workman" who has not been dismissed can file an application under section 34 of the Ordinance. On the other hand, if a worker has been dismissed in connection with or as a consequence of an industrial dispute he cannot maintain an application under that section the bar against the maintainability of such an application comes from the expressions "for the purpose of any proceedings under this Ordinance in relation to an industrial dispute" which are used in the clause defining the second category of workers. The meaning of these expressions become clear when the provisions of section 43 of the Ordinance are considered, This section which provides for the raising of an industrial dispute lays down that no industrial dispute, shall be deemed to exist unless it has been raised in the prescribed manner by a collective bargaining agent or an employer. These provisions therefore, expressly prohibit the raising of an industrial dispute except in the manner mentioned therein. As provided under this section an industrial dispute can be raised by a collective bargaining agent or an employer only in the manner prescribed by the Ordinance. The manner prescribed by the Ordinance for raising an industrial dispute is to be found in the provisions contained in sections 28 to 33 of the Ordinance: No other provisions in the Ordinance deal with the raising of an industrial dispute or prescribe the manner according to which such dispute can be raised, As section 34 does not include any reference to an industrial dispute it cannot, therefore, be said to have prescribed the manner of raising an industrial dispute. It would, therefore, appear that a dismissed worker, who falls within the second part of the definition of "worker" or "workman"in clause (xxviii) of section 2 can bring an application under section 34 for the enforcement of any right guaranteed or secured to him by any law or any award or settlement when an industrial dispute exists which, as already mentioned, can exist, only if it has been raised by a collective bargaining agent or an employer in the manner prescribed by any of the sections, namely, sections 26 to 33 of the Ordinance. During the continuance of such an industrial dispute which led to his dismissal or which arose on his dismissal, a dismissed worker can by filing an application under section 34 enforce any legal right or the term of any award or settlement. If no such dispute exists, a dismissed worker will not fall within the second category of workers or workmen, and he cannot, therefore, maintain an application under section 34. A "worker" or "work-man" who falls in the first category of workers as defined in Clause (xxviii) can, however, maintain an application under section 34, but the first category does not, as mentioned above, include a dismissed worker. 

 27. In order to resolve whether an individual dispute arising out of his dismissal can be decided by the Labour Court on an application of the dismissed worker under section 34, reference has also been made to the definition of an "industrial dispute" as provided in Clause (xiii) of section 2 of the Ordinance. This clause defines an "industrial dispute" as "any dispute or difference between employers and employers or between employers and workmen or between workmen and workmen which is connected' with the employment or non-employment or the terms of employment or the conditions of work of any person". Having regard to this definition it has been claimed that as the dismissal of or any claim made by a dismissed worker relates to his employment or unemployment or the terms of employment or the conditions of work of such a person, any dispute arising from his dismissal or claim made by him will be an, industrial dispute and he can, therefore, bring such dispute to the notice of the Labour Court and ask for its decision under section 34. 

 28. The contrary view is, however, concerned with the interpretation of the other expressions used in the definition such as, "between employers and employers" or "between employers and workmen" or "between workmen and work-men". As the terms, "employers" and "work-men" are expressed in the plural any dispute that may arise between an employer and a single worker cannot be viewed as an industrial dispute, In addition, the scheme and object of the Ordinance would also show that an individual dispute involved the idea of a dispute or difference between the employer and a group or number of workers. According to the learned Advocates for the respondent No. 2 as well as the Amicus Curaie, though the expressions "employers" and "workmen" used in the definition are in the plural, having regard to the provisions of section 13 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, the singular includes a plural and vice-versa. Accordingly, the expression used in the definition being "workmen" it means also a single worker, as the expression "employers" mean a single employer vide, A.I.R. 1953 S.C. 58, A,I.R. 1951 Mad. 616 Various decisions were Cited in support of these conflicting propositions. Apart from these decisions which concern themselves with the contentions whether the plural includes the singular or vice versa, other decisions were cited to show that an individual dispute is an industrial dispute, vide, A.I.R. 1949 Bom. 141, A.I.R. 1949 (F.C.) 111, A.I.R. 1954 All 516, already mentioned above. 

 30. The reasons which prompted the judges to hold that are individual dispute can never be viewed as an industrial dispute were that if this were possible the whole purpose and scheme of the legislation which provided for the settlement of an industrial dispute will be defeated. After the enactment of the Ordinance of 1969 these decisions, as pointed out by the learned Additional Attorney-General, find additional support from the provisions of section 43 of the Ordinance. As already seen, this section contains an express prohibition against the raising of an industrial dispute except by a collective bargaining agent or an employer or except in the manner prescribed/in the Ordinance. The prohibition against raising an industrial dispute as provided by this section cannot be nullified by anything contained in section 34 which does not specifically contain any words or expressions showing that such a dispute can be raised under that section. Even such expressions as "any party to an industrial dispute" or "adjudication of the dispute" as occurred in the unamended section 34 which might have been viewed as nullifying the intention of the legislature as expressed in section 43, do no longer exist. The aforesaid expressions have been omitted from the amended section 34. There is no other phrase or clause in section 34 which can be interpreted as nullifying the express prohibition in section 43 of the Ordinance. It is difficult to understand how, m the absence of any exception, the express prohibition imposed by section 43 can be overcome on or importance be whittled down. Even if it be conceded that an individual dispute between a single worker and his employer can be included within the definition of "industrial dispute", such dispute cannot, I am afraid, be brought to the notice of the Labour Court for its decision by reason of the express prohibition contained in section 43 of the Ordinance. Being unqualified the prohibition must seem to be both total and complete. 

 31. Neither can the express prohibition against the raising of an industrial dispute except in the prescribed manner by the collective bargaining agent or the employer be circumvented or overcome by the provisions relating to the commencement of the proceedings before a Labour Court as provided in clause (a) of sub-section (3) of section 41 of the Ordinance. Clause (a) of this sub-section runs as follows: 

 (a) in relation to an industrial dispute, on the date on which an application has been made 	under section 32 or section 34, or on the date on which it is referred to the Labour Court by the Government under section 32 or section 33 ; and 

 32.With regard to the expressions "in relation to an industrial dispute" as used in this clause, it has been claimed that an application under' section 34 which commences on the date it is filed invariably relates to and involves an industrial dispute. This would not seem acceptable for two reasons. First, this clause does not expressly provide an exception to the bar imposed by section 43 against raising an industrial dispute in a manner other than what has been prescribed by the Ordinance. Secondly, an application under section 34 which is filed "in relation to an industrial dispute" does not mean that it involves an industrial dispute. An individual dispute which may arise during the continuation of, or in relation to an industrial dispute may be brought to the notice of a Labour Court by filing an application under section 34 which shall be deemed "in relation to an industrial dispute" and to have commenced on the date on which it is made. The provisions of clause (a) of sub-section (3) of section 41 of the Ordinance do not, therefore, seem to be in conflict with those of section 43 of the Ordinance. In support of the contention that an individual dispute which is an industrial dispute can be brought before the Labour Court by a single worker under section 34 of the Ordinance, reliance was also placed On the provisions of section 35(5) (a) of the Ordinance. Clause (a) of this Sub-section provides as follows: 

 (a) Adjudicate and determine an industrial dispute which has been referred to or brought before it under this Ordinance. " 

 33. It has been submitted that this clause is the only provision in the Ordinance which has conferred jurisdiction on the Labour Court "to adjudicate and determine an industrial dispute", thereby implying that section 34 did not create such jurisdiction. It has been claimed that section 34 merely enabled one of the three categories of persons mentioned there in to bring its or his dispute before the Labour Court. As soon as an application is made under this section by a dismissed worker. the Labour Court, it was claimed, gets jurisdiction to decide such application as an industrial dispute only because clause (a) of section 35(5) empowered the Labour, Court to decide such dispute. Great emphasis was put upon the difference of meaning between the two sets of expressions used in this clause. The expressions "brought before it" used in this clause were relied upon in support of the view that an individual dispute by a single worker cannot be "referred to" but can be "brought before" the Labour Court by filing an application under section 34 of the Ordinance All other  industrial disputes which are raised under sections 26 to 33 of the Ordinance are "referred to" and not "brought before it". The expressions "referred to" relate to such industrial disputes which are raised in the manner laid down in the aforesaid sections, namely, sections 26 to 32. It was also submitted that since the amended section 35(5)(a) does no longer expressly refer to section 34, the jurisdiction to decide an application under section 34 can only be derived from clause (a) of section 35(5) of the Ordinance. I do not think that the omission of any reference to section 34 from the amended clause (a) of section 35(5) has conferred any jurisdiction on the Labour Court to decide an individual dispute under that clause, On the contrary, the express omission of all references to section 34 and the repeal of the expressions "relating to a matter in respect of which an application is made to it under section 34" from clause (a) shows the positive intention of the legislature that the Labour Court will not, while proceeding under this clause, decide an application under section 34. It does not seem convincing to me that without, any express mention of section 34 in the provisions of section 35 conferring jurisdictional Labour Court it cannot decide an application under the former section. Nor am I willing to accept the submission made by the learned, Additional Attorney-General that clause (d) of section 35(5) confers the necessary Jurisdiction upon the Labour Court to, decide an application under section 34. Clause (d) of this sub-section enables the Labour Court to exercise other powers and functions under the Ordinance. It seems to me that general jurisdiction to decide an industrial dispute has been conferred by clause (a) of sub-section (5) of section 35 but this sub-section. has not either expressly or impliedly negatived the power of the Labour Court to decide an individual dispute by a single worker under section 34, Section 35 is not nor can It be deemed to be the only provision conferring jurisdiction upon the Labour Court to decide a dispute. The provisions of section 34 which enable the persons mentioned therein to apply to the Labour Court are both enable self-contained as well as clear and the expressions "may apply to the Labour Court for the enforcement of any right", are sufficient to enable the Labour Court to operate and, therefore, adjudicate any dispute presented for its determination by such application. No further, conferment of jurisdiction on' the Labour Court under sub-section, (5) of section 35 is necessary.

Finally, there is, no doubt, some substance in the contention that since the definition of "worker" as provided in section 2(v) of-the Act of 1965 is narrower than that given in the Ordinance, (here any person who does not fall with in the definition of "employer" is a worker) a large number of persons who will be excluded from the former definition and will, therefore, be unable to maintain an application under section 25 of the Act of 1965 when an order of dismissal is passed by the employer against anyone or all of them. But this difficulty, even if it. may seem to be insurmountable, does not defy all solutions, and it cannot, therefore, be pleaded as a ground for holding that a dismissed worker is entitled to challenge the legality of his dismissal under section 34 of the Ordinance, and such individual dispute must, therefore, be regarded as an industrial dispute so as to enable them to maintain such an application. A dismissed worker who falls within the definition of "worker" in the Act of 1965,to respondent No.2 is within such a definition can avail of the procedure laid down in section 25 of the Act of 1915 for challenging his dismissal. A dismissed worker who is not included within the narrower definition of "worker" as provided in the Act of 1965 will not, however, be without any legal remedy, though unable to seek the protection against dismissal under section 25.
